To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the climate forcing needed to collapse the THC is uncertain, but (ii) a THC tipping point is likely, (iii) some early warning of the proximity of a tipping point appears possible, and (iv) a collapse of the THC is irreversible.

(i) there are two stable states of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) in a hierarchy of coupled ocean–atmospheremodels; (ii) the probability of a collapse of the AMOC increases with anthropogenic climate forcing; and (iii) some ensemble members of the AMOC collapse readily, whereas other ensemble members are extremely resistant.

‘The Atlantic thermohalinc circulation (THC) is an archetypal tipping element in the climate system, and the proximity of the climate system to a tipping point in THC is detectable from the time series of the THC.’
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of tipping points in the climate system, and the use of eScience tools and methods to study them.
the question of how we might detect and respond to a climate system that has passed a threshold, and is in danger of crossing another.
the development and application of new techniques in eScience to study a critical issue in the climate sciences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a THC tipping point may be imminent, but that it could also be decades away.
the climate system is complex and that the future is uncertain.
the probability of crossing the THC bifurcation point is increasing, but the time scale is still uncertain, and the irreversibility is also uncertain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of GENIE has been a key factor in our ability to study the THC tipping point problem and to understand the role of the atmosphere in the THC.
the climate system is highly nonlinear and the climate response to anthropogenic forcing may be highly uncertain.
the climate system has a rich repertoire of dynamical behaviour, which can be studied using eScience methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eScience can be very useful in studying the climate system, and in particular tipping points.
the climate system is complex and that the use of a hierarchy of models is essential to understanding the system’s response to climate change.
, with the help of eScience, the study of tipping points in the climate system is now possible and is likely to lead to new insights into how climate change might unfold in the future.
